endorsements.quote: We suggest developing risk-tiered guidelines, where human oversight is proportionate to potential patient harm.

This includes training on the ethical use of AI, data governance, and cybersecurity, ensuring that health care providers can confidently integrate AI into their practices while adhering to regulatory requirements [ 22 ].
To equip health care professionals with the knowledge and skills needed to understand and work alongside AI systems, investment in AI literacy could be beneficial.

Policymakers must anticipate these secondary effects when promoting AI adoption and consider protective strategies such as retraining programs, mental health support, and frameworks for meaningful human-machine collaboration in clinical settings.

Future iterations of the AI Act and related frameworks could benefit from incorporating sustainability criteria—such as lifecycle assessments, emissions reporting, or green AI standards—to ensure that health innovation does not inadvertently generate new public health risks through environmental degradation.
This includes public reporting of algorithmic impact assessments, bias audits, and governance structures—similar to financial disclosures.
Procurement policies can also serve as a powerful lever: health care systems can favor vendors that demonstrate ethical compliance, much like environmental or labor standards in other sectors [ 31 ].

unlisted_practices: Establish multidisciplinary national or regional task forces of AI experts, clinicians, ethicists, and legal scholars to advise regulators on bottlenecks in implementing the AI Act.
Create regulatory sandboxes that pilot health care AI under temporary regulatory flexibility with close authority oversight.
Develop modular, localizable AI training curricula with EU-level minimum competency standards and open-access multilingual materials.
Build geopolitically resilient supply chains for medical devices and AI technologies by diversifying suppliers, incentivizing dual-sourcing, and developing contingency plans.
Foster international collaboration on AI standards and ethics through WHO, OECD, and G7/G20 forums without ceding national control.
Verify AI-generated responses in high-stakes clinical applications through vetted peer clinician consultants (human-in-the-loop).
Establish clear ethical guidelines for health care AI use, addressing bias, transparency, and accountability, especially in high-stakes scenarios such as triage during conflicts or pandemics.
Co-develop ethical guidelines with industry stakeholders.

screen.reason: Analysis and commentary on the EU AI Act's regulatory requirements, compliance burdens, and policy recommendations for governing AI in healthcare.
